opus-5.5.text:
I think it's hard because a world model, at its core, isn't really a product — it's a capability. It's closer to something like "understanding" or "intelligence" itself. With large language models, we got lucky in a way: language is already the interface humans use to communicate, so the moment the model got good enough, the chatbot was a very natural product form. You type, it answers. The capability and the product almost collapsed into the same thing.

For world models, there's no such obvious collapse. What does it mean to "use" a model that understands physics, space, causality, how objects persist and interact? You could say video generation — but generating pretty pixels is really just one surface manifestation, and honestly not even the most important one. A model can produce visually stunning video and still not understand the world in any deep sense. So if you anchor the product on generation, you might end up optimizing for the wrong thing.

Then there are the other candidates: robotics, autonomous driving, simulation for training agents, games, AR glasses, spatial intelligence for some kind of embodied assistant. Each of these is real, but each is also either very far from mature, or very fragmented, or the world model is just one component inside a much larger system. None of them yet feels like "this is the ChatGPT moment for world models."

And there's a deeper tension. As a researcher, I believe the real value of a world model is in planning and reasoning — being able to imagine consequences before acting, the way humans and animals do. That's an internal capability. It may not be something you directly see. So the ultimate product might be something where the world model is invisible, sitting underneath an agent that just behaves more intelligently in the physical world. But building that agent requires solving many other problems at the same time — hardware, data, control, safety.

So it's hard partly because the technology isn't there yet, but also because we may still be asking the question in the wrong frame. We tend to look for the next product by analogy with the last one. I suspect the right product for world models will look quite different, and we probably won't fully recognize it until the capability matures enough that it almost reveals itself.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs benefited because language is a familiar human interface, making the chatbot a natural product as soon as the model was capable enough.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's hard because the technology and the product are evolving at the same time, and neither one is settled. With language models, there was a kind of lucky alignment: the model predicts text, and humans already communicate in text, so a chat box turned out to be a surprisingly natural interface. The product almost fell out of the capability. For world models, we don't have that gift. A world model, as I think about it, is a system that builds an internal representation of the physical world, of space, time, objects, dynamics, and can use that to predict, simulate, and eventually act. That's a very general capability, and generality is exactly what makes the product question hard.

If you ask people what the product is, you get completely different answers depending on who you ask. The robotics people say it's a simulator for training policies. The graphics and gaming people say it's an infinite, interactive game engine. The video people say it's a generation tool. Some people say it's the foundation for embodied agents, for a robot in your home. All of those are plausible, but they pull the research in different directions. A video generation product rewards visual fidelity, and you can get very far with something that looks right without being physically consistent. A robotics product rewards the opposite: it can look ugly, but the physics and the long-horizon consistency have to be correct, because you're going to act on it. So the question of "what is the product" is really the question of "what is the objective," and we don't agree on that yet.

There's also a deeper issue, which is that for world models we don't even have a good way to measure progress. With language you can at least look at benchmarks, however imperfect they are. For a world model, how do you evaluate whether the model actually understands the world versus just producing plausible-looking pixels? I think a lot of the current work is still stuck in the generation framing, where the output is a video and the metric is whether a human thinks it looks good. That's not the same as understanding. If the product is defined by that metric, I worry we end up optimizing for the wrong thing.

And honestly, part of it is that the "ultimate product" might not be a single product at all. Maybe it's more like an operating layer, something that sits underneath many applications, the way a physics engine sits under many games. That's a very different business and a very different research agenda than a consumer app. So when people ask me what the killer app for world models is, my honest answer is that I think we have to let the capability mature a bit more before we can see it clearly. The risk is that we lock in a product definition too early, based on what looks impressive today, and that definition constrains what the model becomes. That's why I see it as a hard problem, not just an engineering problem but a problem of deciding what we're even building.

r001.rationale: The response links LLMs’ success to the natural fit between text prediction and human communication, saying this made a chat box a surprisingly natural interface.

astra-6.text:
I think the hard part is that a world model is a capability, but it isn’t yet a product definition. You can say, “I want a model that understands how the world evolves and can predict what happens next.” That’s a compelling research goal. But who needs that prediction, what decision does it help them make, and how reliable does it have to be? Those questions depend very much on the application.

For example, generating a plausible future and predicting the consequences of an action are different requirements. If you’re creating entertainment, a plausible result might be enough. If you’re using the model to guide a robot, looking plausible isn’t enough—you need the consequences to be right. So even deciding what counts as a good world model requires some understanding of the product.

That creates a kind of circular problem. We want the capability to reveal new applications, but we also need applications to tell us which capabilities to build and how to evaluate them. I think that’s why finding the ultimate product is so difficult. You have to discover a useful interaction between the model and a real need, and that doesn’t automatically follow from making the model more powerful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses world models and product applications; it does not attribute LLM success to a chatbot interface.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hard part is that “world model” describes a capability, but it doesn’t yet tell you what the product should be. What does the user actually want to do with that capability? Do they want to generate a video, explore an interactive environment, or have a system help them plan an action? Those lead to very different requirements.

If you’re generating a video, looking plausible might be enough. But if you’re using the model to make decisions, you need to know whether it understands how the world responds to your actions. A prediction can look convincing and still be wrong in a way that matters.

So there are two uncertainties together: how to build the capability, and where that capability creates enough value for someone to use it repeatedly. You need the application to tell you what to optimize, but you also need a sufficiently capable model to discover which applications are possible. That makes finding the product a very difficult process.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about world-model capabilities and product applications, but it does not attribute LLM success to the chatbot interface.
